rv.q: Joe (George Naylor) is a cynical gay ‘actor’ – inverted commas because in reality he works in a shitty pub while not getting any acting work. He’s on the cusp of trying to get a real job when one of the regulars – a handsome, aloof man named David who Joe dubs ‘the mysterious stranger’ – asks if Joe could do a gig at his country estate.
Around the House At Night is a deliciously spine-tingling triumph of stagecraft.
The result is an engrossing, intriguing and highly entertaining show that steadily builds suspense and uses its narrator to balance plausibility and incredulity.

As the ghost story elements continue, Foley’s script also explores Joe’s backstory, especially his relationship with his ex, who turns out to come from the sort of hereditary wealth mirroring that of the family who owned Paragon Hall. There is a sense that the demonic forces Joe encounters convey metaphors on multiple levels.

There’s some great stage trickery deployed on the set designed by Tom Robbins and director Neil Bettles, which ensures that the impacts of lighting and video projection by Joshua Pharo are fully maximised.
An impressive and energetic production that doesn't rely on suddenly cranking up the volume to make patrons jump – it's far more slick and sophisticated than that.
The humour undermines the horror, and a slew of anecdotes about his work and love life mean the whole thing lacks immediacy.
It’s unclear why this pamphleteering drivel is being presented as a ghost story.

cn.t: Critics praise this spine-tingling horror play as a triumph of stagecraft that capitalizes on the genre's resurgence, though some note it shows its hand too eagerly and over-explains the mystery.
